newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA KATZ COMMISSION BACKS CAPITAL TRANSFER TAX.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA KATZ COMMISSION BACKS CAPITAL TRANSFER TAX.

text.p: The Commission of Inquiry into aspects of South Africa's tax structure has recommended the country should have a capital transfer tax -- a form of tax which already exists and which should be retained.

In its fourth interim report, the commission, headed by Michael Katz, said that while there were disadvantages to such a tax, there were compelling reasons in the South African context to justify its retention.
Disadvantages to capital transfer tax included the fact that it had a notoriously low yield, was extremely complex and had also given rise to an unproductive estate planning industry.
However, South Africa was characterised by a marked concentration of wealth.
"Thus, even if income tax were levied on saved income and capital gains, inheritances would remain as an untaxed item in the absence of capital transfer taxes," it said.
"Similarly, inter vivos gifts would escape taxation which would, in the context of South Africa, raise serious questions about the equity of the tax system," it said.

South Africa has a flat rate of tax applicable to both donations and estates, currently 25 percent, with relief on a sliding scale where the same asset is taxable twice by reason of a second death occuring within 10 years of a preceding death.
Of these, there is a 25,000 rand rebate on donations and a one million rand rebate on estate duty.
The commission said that in its view, the donations tax should be retained, while the system of estate duty should be retained instead of an inheritance tax being introduced.
It said an appropriate rate of capital transfer tax was a policy decision that had to be taken by government.
While rebate levels were also a policy decision, the commission said it was considered that existing rebates should continue to remain in force, it said.
